concept: Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements
summary: Source-anchored research for Parkinson's disease rehabilitation and adjunct therapies: exercise, physical, speech and occupational therapy, dance, music, acupuncture, cannabis and supplements. Run status: COMPLETED.

narrative.documentConcept: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
narrative.text: Evidence read for acupuncture, massage, the Alexander Technique and other traditional adjuncts in Parkinson's disease (PD). Two older meta-analyses found no significant UPDRS advantage of real over placebo acupuncture; later syntheses of acupuncture combined with conventional treatment report UPDRS gains but describe the evidence as limited, and an overview rated all included reviews very-low-quality. Sham-controlled trials show a sleep signal and no fatigue benefit over sham. No serious adverse events were reported. Massage meta-analyses report motor benefit alongside methodological concerns. NICE NG71 says to consider the Alexander Technique for balance or motor function problems; a complementary-medicine guideline grades acupuncture added to drugs 'should be considered' on low-level evidence; Parkinson's UK does not endorse any particular therapies.

narrative.documentConcept: Acupuncture, massage and traditional adjuncts in PD
narrative.text: Kluger et al. and Kong et al. attribute the improvement seen in both arms of sham-controlled fatigue trials to nonspecific or placebo effects, while Kwon et al. suggest a sham acupuncture-controlled design might underestimate the effect of acupuncture treatment.

narrative.text: For electroacupuncture, the Cho et al. guideline reports no significant difference in overall clinical effectiveness in three RCTs, whereas Yu et al. report that electroacupuncture showed the highest overall efficacy among all modalities.

narrative.documentConcept: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
narrative.text: Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of cannabis and cannabinoids in Parkinson's disease (PD), published 2022 to 2026, report that the evidence does not establish clinical benefit. Individual randomized trials of CBD/THC oils, CBD and nabilone are small and heterogeneous: the Colorado CBD/THC trial and the 2026 São Paulo cannabis-oil trial found no significant difference on their primary outcomes, while one nabilone trial reported a non-motor symptom difference. Reported adverse events include dizziness, confusion and irritability. Positive effects described in uncontrolled studies were not confirmed by small RCTs, per one review. The Parkinson's Foundation does not endorse use for PD symptoms or disease progression. One phase II CBD trial was listed as recruiting in the registry.

narrative.documentConcept: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
narrative.text: Levodopa-induced dyskinesia: Sieradzan et al. report that nabilone significantly reduced it in a crossover trial (n = 7), while Carroll et al. report no treatment effect of oral cannabis extract in a crossover trial.

narrative.documentConcept: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD
narrative.text: Non-motor symptoms: Peball et al. report a MDS-UPDRS-I difference with nabilone, while Kubota et al. report no significant differences for CBD/THC oil in other non-motor scales.

narrative.documentConcept: Cannabis and cannabinoids in PD

narrative.documentConcept: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs
narrative.text: Group-based exercise modes in Parkinson's disease are described by guidelines and reviews with mixed strength. The APTA guideline gives community-based exercise a strong recommendation with high evidence strength, while the European guideline gives only weak recommendations for dance and a strong one for tai chi on UPDRS III. Randomized trials report better limits-of-stability with tai chi than resistance training or stretching and better MDS-UPDRS-3 with 12 months of tango than no intervention. Meta-analyses diverge on quality of life for tai chi and qigong, on yoga robustness, on Nordic walking benefit and on boxing, and review authors describe dance evidence as low certainty or critically low confidence.

narrative.documentConcept: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs
narrative.text: The APTA guideline cites its reference 174, the Combs et al. randomized trial, among studies indicating superior balance outcomes for boxing over traditional multi-modal exercise, whereas that trial's abstract reports that the traditional exercise group had significantly greater gains in balance confidence than the boxing group.

narrative.documentConcept: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs
narrative.text: On dance and motor symptom severity, the European guideline gives a weak recommendation against dance for UPDRS III while two dance meta-analyses report better MDS-UPDRS III scores with dance than with no intervention.

narrative.documentConcept: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs
narrative.text: Tai chi and qigong meta-analyses disagree on quality of life: Song et al. report an improvement while Fidan et al. and a later traditional Chinese exercise meta-analysis report no significant effect.

narrative.documentConcept: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs
narrative.text: Boxing reviews disagree: Wang et al. report effective improvement of motor and non-motor symptoms while Gonzalez-Devesa et al. and Hernandez-Martinez et al. report no significant pooled effects.

narrative.documentConcept: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs
narrative.text: Yoga meta-analyses report benefit, but a network meta-analysis found the significant effects of yoga not robust in sensitivity analysis.

narrative.documentConcept: Dance, tai chi, yoga, boxing and community exercise programs
narrative.text: Nordic walking reviews differ: Salse-Batán et al. report no clinically meaningful benefits except walking ability while De Santis and Kaplan report consistent improvement in symptom severity, walking speed and gait pattern.

narrative.text: Whether the percentages printed in the Pinto et al. abstract (69%, 9%, 2% and 13% for 55 reviews) are internally consistent with the stated review counts.

narrative.text: Whether the 12-month tango result on MDS-UPDRS-3 replicates in a design with an active comparator, since the control group in the Duncan and Earhart trial received no intervention.

narrative.documentConcept: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
narrative.text: Guidelines read here (NICE NG71, the APTA physical therapist guideline and the German Society for Neurology guideline) include physiotherapy statements. APTA grades aerobic exercise, resistance training and balance training as high evidence quality with strong recommendations, and flexibility exercises as low and weak. A Cochrane network meta-analysis of 154 RCTs reported benefits for most exercise types, little evidence of differences between types, and confidence from moderate to very low. Sources differ on quality-of-life effects and on high versus moderate intensity, and the PD REHAB trial found no difference in its primary outcome for physiotherapy plus occupational therapy. Reviews describe follow-up evidence as short, and sources differ on whether exercise slows progression. SPARX3, a phase 3 high-intensity treadmill trial, was listed as active, not recruiting, with no results posted.

narrative.documentConcept: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
narrative.text: Quality-of-life findings differ: APTA, the Cochrane network meta-analysis and Radder report improvements for some interventions, while PD REHAB, the earlier Cochrane review and Shu report no significant difference.

narrative.documentConcept: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
narrative.text: High versus moderate intensity: the SPARX phase 2 trial reported only its high-intensity arm reached the nonfutility threshold, while a systematic review found no statistically significant difference between vigorous and moderate or low intensity.

narrative.documentConcept: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
narrative.text: Progression: the Parkinson's Foundation page states consistent exercise can slow symptom progression, while the APTA guideline states it is not clear whether the effects of aerobic exercise are disease modifying.

narrative.documentConcept: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
narrative.text: Certainty: APTA labels aerobic exercise and resistance training evidence quality high with strong recommendations, while the Cochrane network meta-analysis rates confidence low for endurance and strength/resistance training on motor-sign severity.

narrative.documentConcept: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
narrative.text: Whether and when SPARX3 will report its 12-month MDS-UPDRS Part III result: the registry record lists primary completion as estimated 2027-07-31 and no results posted.

narrative.documentConcept: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
narrative.text: Whether exercise slows disease progression rather than only benefiting symptoms: the APTA guideline says this is not clear and Crotty and Schwarzschild list it as an outstanding question.

narrative.documentConcept: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
narrative.text: Which exercise intensity and dose is best: the APTA guideline says the optimal dosing of aerobic exercise has not been determined, and a systematic review of vigorous-intensity exercise called the evidence too limited to allow recommendations.

narrative.documentConcept: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
narrative.text: Long-term effects of physiotherapy and exercise: the physiotherapy meta-analysis by Radder and colleagues stated that it was not possible to perform a meta-analysis on long-term effects.

narrative.documentConcept: Exercise and physical therapy in PD
narrative.text: The APTA guideline databases were last searched on June 16, 2020 and the Cochrane network meta-analysis searched to 17 May 2021; whether later syntheses alter their conclusions is not established here.

narrative.documentConcept: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
narrative.text: LSVT LOUD and LSVT BIG are standardized, intensive programmes (16 sessions over four weeks) that train the amplitude of voice or limb movement. In the PD COMM trial of 388 people, LSVT LOUD lowered self-reported voice handicap versus no therapy and versus NHS speech and language therapy, with benefit still present at 12 months and mostly minor vocal-strain adverse events. Two Cochrane reviews (searches to April 2011) found insufficient evidence; later meta-analyses report higher vocal loudness, while intelligibility results are mixed. NICE NG71 recommends speech and language therapy including attention to effort therapies; RCSLT guidance (December 2025) highly recommends LSVT LOUD. For LSVT BIG, the Berlin trial reported UPDRS motor gains, but a meta-analysis found only trends for walking and rated evidence preliminary.

narrative.documentConcept: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
narrative.text: Session length for LSVT LOUD differs by source: Ramig and colleagues describe 16 individual 1-hour sessions in 1 month, whereas PD COMM and the Dutch guideline describe 50-minute sessions four times a week for four weeks.

narrative.documentConcept: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
narrative.text: The Constantinescu abstract reports non-significant main effects for the LSVT environment, dysarthria severity and interaction effects for all outcome measures, whereas the Cochrane review states that sustained phonation loudness did not support the equivalence of online and face-to-face delivery and was significant in favour of face-to-face delivery.

narrative.documentConcept: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
narrative.text: NICE NG71 recommendation 1.7.8 gives attention to effort therapies as its example of speech and communication strategies, whereas RCSLT guidance (December 2025) states that LSVT LOUD is the only behavioural treatment with strong evidence for managing dysarthria.

narrative.documentConcept: LSVT BIG, LSVT LOUD and speech-language therapy
narrative.text: Parkinson's UK says questionnaires were completed at 3, 6 and 9 months, whereas the BMJ trial report says follow-up was at three, six, and 12 months after randomisation.

narrative.documentConcept: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
narrative.text: Educational summary of what published sources say, not medical advice. Meta-analyses of rhythmic auditory stimulation and music-based interventions in Parkinson's disease report positive pooled effects on gait velocity and stride length but not cadence, and disagree on balance, timed up-and-go, UPDRS motor scores and freezing of gait. One singing review rates the certainty of its RCT-based finding as very low and another calls singing a promising adjunct therapy, and a trial's own authors limit attribution to singing. Reviews conflict on quality of life, mood and cognition. The visual art therapy evidence cited here is an exploratory observational study, and a meta-analysis calls visual arts and painting a research gap; one art-therapy meta-analysis of 26 trials included 14 dance trials. Review authors repeatedly flag small samples and limited blinding.

narrative.documentConcept: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
narrative.text: Balance and timed up-and-go: Wang and colleagues report statistically significant pooled improvements, while Ye and colleagues report no significant pooled difference for either.

narrative.documentConcept: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
narrative.text: UPDRS motor score and freezing of gait: one meta-analysis (K = 6 studies, total N = 168) found no significant effects, while Ye and colleagues report significant improvements in UPDRS-III and the Freezing of Gait Questionnaire.

narrative.documentConcept: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
narrative.text: Quality of life, cognition and mood: Lee and Ko report no significant pooled effects on quality of life and cognition and Liu and colleagues report no significant pooled effects on quality of life, cognition or depressive symptoms, while a music-therapy meta-analysis of thirty-three studies reports significant improvements in depression, anxiety and life quality.

narrative.documentConcept: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
narrative.text: Singing: Irons and Sheffield state they are unable to determine the effects of singing interventions, while Trinchillo and colleagues conclude that singing is a promising adjunct therapy.

narrative.documentConcept: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
narrative.text: Parkinsonics: Trinchillo and colleagues state that Butala and colleagues found significant motor improvements after 24 weeks, while Butala and colleagues state they cannot conclusively attribute motor improvements to the singing intervention.

narrative.documentConcept: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
narrative.text: Whether the music-therapy meta-analysis of thirty-three studies including 3635 patients is supported on full-text review is not established here, because only its PubMed abstract is in the pinned body.

narrative.documentConcept: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
narrative.text: Whether differences in the included trials explain why Wang and colleagues and Ye and colleagues disagree on balance and timed up-and-go results is not established by the pinned text.

narrative.documentConcept: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
narrative.text: Whether benefits persist after interventions end: Pohl and colleagues report between-group differences in the Falls Efficacy Scale and Parkinson Disease Questionnaire-39 items that were not maintained at three months post-intervention, while Butala and colleagues report that some improvements were sustained at least six weeks after interventions ended.

narrative.documentConcept: Music, art and creative therapies in PD
narrative.text: Which randomized trials of visual art therapy in Parkinson's disease exist beyond the exploratory observational study of eighteen patients, given the meta-analysis authors' statement that visual arts and painting represent a significant research gap.

narrative.documentConcept: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
narrative.text: What published sources report about occupational therapy, external cueing and gait training in Parkinson's disease. NICE guideline NG71 and an AOTA practice guideline address occupational therapy. The OTiP trial reported a favourable primary outcome, the PD REHAB trial reported no difference on its primary outcome, and a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence. The APTA guideline rates external cueing and gait training as high evidence quality with strong recommendation strength, yet meta-analyses differ on the best cue modality, and a 2026 meta-analysis found no significant reduction in freezing-of-gait severity. Treadmill meta-analyses report improved walking speed but not cadence. Authors describe cueing durability as unclear and wearable cueing as evaluated mainly in laboratories. This is an attributed summary of sources, not medical advice.

narrative.documentConcept: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
narrative.text: OTiP reported a favourable primary outcome for home-based occupational therapy at 3 months, whereas PD REHAB reported no difference in its primary outcome for physiotherapy plus occupational therapy versus no therapy.

narrative.documentConcept: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
narrative.text: The APTA guideline recommends external cueing to reduce freezing of gait, whereas a 2026 meta-analysis of repeated external cueing found no statistically significant reduction in FOG severity.

narrative.documentConcept: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
narrative.text: Cue modality: a 2013 meta-analysis favoured auditory cueing, a 2026 network meta-analysis reported that somatosensory and visual cues outperformed standalone auditory stimulation, and a 2024 review found that adding visual cueing to walking training did not improve walking speed or stride length.

narrative.documentConcept: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
narrative.text: Cadence: a 2013 meta-analysis reported significant improvement of cadence with auditory cueing (Hedge g=.556), whereas Ghai et al. reported a negative effect on cadence with application of auditory cueing.

narrative.documentConcept: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
narrative.text: Treadmill gait-speed effect size: the Cochrane review reported MD = 0.09 m/s, whereas a second meta-analysis reported MD 0.21m/second for comfortable walking velocity.

narrative.documentConcept: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
narrative.text: Evidence quality for cueing: the APTA guideline gives evidence quality as high, whereas Nascimento et al. describe low-quality evidence that adding auditory cueing to walking training improves walking speed.

narrative.documentConcept: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
narrative.text: Has APTA revised, reaffirmed or withdrawn its Parkinson disease guideline? The guideline states that in 5 years it will either be revised, reaffirmed or withdrawn.

narrative.documentConcept: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
narrative.text: PubMed lists errata for the OTiP Lancet Neurology article (Lancet Neurol 2014 Jun;13(6):536 and 2016 Mar;15(3):241); their content was not read, so their effect on the reported numbers is not established.

narrative.documentConcept: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
narrative.text: The Cochrane occupational therapy review read here has electronic searches up to April 2007; whether a later Cochrane update exists was not established.

narrative.documentConcept: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
narrative.text: The APTA guideline states that no studies were identified that investigated the effects of external cueing on fall rate or number of falls; whether later trials report fall outcomes was not established.

narrative.documentConcept: Occupational therapy, cueing and gait training
narrative.text: The 2026 freezing-of-gait meta-analysis restricts to repeated external cueing interventions of 2 weeks or more and reports substantial heterogeneity; whether its difference from the APTA statement reflects study selection, outcome measures or cueing protocols is not established by the sources read.

narrative.documentConcept: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants
narrative.text: Trial evidence for supplements and failed neuroprotectants in Parkinson disease is largely negative in the sources read. Large trials of coenzyme Q10 (QE3), creatine (NET-PD LS-1), inosine (SURE-PD3) and isradipine (STEADY-PD III) each reported no clinical benefit, as did a tocopherol trial. Earlier signals, a CoQ10 dosage-ranging trial reporting a positive trend and a creatine futility screen that did not reject it, were followed by later large trials reporting no benefit. Vitamin D reports are mixed. Mucuna pruriens trials are small and short, and commercial products varied widely from labelled levodopa. NICE NG71 recommends against vitamin E and, except in the context of clinical trials, against co-enzyme Q10 as neuroprotective therapy, recommends that creatine supplements not be offered, and advises a vitamin D supplement. This summarizes what sources report; it is not medical advice.

narrative.documentConcept: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants
narrative.text: A 2002 CoQ10 dosage-ranging trial reported a significant 1200-mg/d versus placebo difference (P =.04) and concluded CoQ10 appears to slow functional decline, while the 2014 QE3 phase III trial reported no evidence of clinical benefit.

narrative.documentConcept: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants
narrative.text: The 2026 review describes the NET-PD creatine trial as randomizing nearly 1000 participants, whereas the JAMA report gives 1741 participants and a futility analysis of 955.

narrative.documentConcept: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants
narrative.text: A 2013 trial reported that vitamin D3 prevented Hoehn and Yahr stage deterioration, while a 2026 trial reported no significant improvement in motor function with vitamin D3.

narrative.documentConcept: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants
narrative.text: The STEADY-PD III report concluded that immediate-release isradipine did not slow clinical progression, while a re-analysis of STEADY-PD II data concluded that clinically attainable brain exposure to isradipine may slow early-stage PD progression.

narrative.documentConcept: Supplements: CoQ10, creatine, vitamin D, Mucuna and failed neuroprotectants
narrative.text: A 2025 systematic review associated Mucuna pruriens with fewer adverse events, while a 12-month open-label trial reported adverse events were more frequent with Mucuna pruriens (56% vs. 37.5%, p = 0.48).
